branch_push.all.failed.one: Pushing {branch} failed on {remotes} ({count} of {total} remotes). The log shows why.
branch_push.all.failed.other: Pushing {branch} failed on {remotes} ({count} of {total} remotes). The log shows why.
branch_push.force.body.gone: As last fetched, {upstream} isn't on {remote}, so force pushing creates it from {branch}.
branch_push.force.body.lease: If {upstream} has moved since the last fetch, the push is refused and nothing is overwritten.
branch_push.force.body.none: As last fetched, {upstream} has no commits that {branch} doesn't have. Force pushing replaces {upstream} with {branch}.
branch_push.force.body.one: {upstream} has {count} commit that {branch} doesn't have. Force pushing replaces {upstream} with {branch}, and that commit is no longer on {remote}.
branch_push.force.body.other: {upstream} has {count} commits that {branch} doesn't have. Force pushing replaces {upstream} with {branch}, and those commits are no longer on {remote}.
branch_push.force.default: {branch} is the default branch of {remote}, so it is never force pushed: others build on it.
branch_push.force.development: Git Flow uses {branch} as its development branch, so it is never force pushed.
branch_push.force.moved: {upstream} moved since you confirmed, so {branch} wasn't force pushed. Look at its new commits, then try again.
branch_push.force.no_upstream: {branch} has no upstream on a remote to force push to.
branch_push.force.production: Git Flow uses {branch} as its production branch, so it is never force pushed.
branch_push.force.title: Force push {branch}
branch_push.force.upstream_changed: The upstream of {branch} is no longer {upstream}, so it wasn't force pushed. Look at its new upstream, then try again.
branch_push.force.warn.default: {dest} is the default branch of {remote}, which others build on: this overwrites {upstream} with your local {branch}.
branch_push.force.warn.development: Git Flow uses {base} as its development branch: this overwrites {upstream} with your local {branch}.
branch_push.force.warn.production: Git Flow uses {base} as its production branch: this overwrites {upstream} with your local {branch}.
branch_push.plain.behind: {branch} is behind {dest}, so git would reject the push. Bring in {dest}'s commits first, or force push.
branch_push.plain.invalid: push.default is set to "{value}", which git doesn't accept (nothing, current, upstream, simple or matching), so git refuses to push. Fix push.default in your git config.
branch_push.plain.name_differs: {branch} tracks {upstream}, which has another name, so a plain git push (push.default is simple) refuses it. Use Push to {remote} to update {upstream}, or set push.default to upstream.
branch_push.plain.no_remote: {remote} isn't a remote in this repository, so git has nowhere to push {branch}. Set another upstream.
branch_push.plain.not_in_refspecs: remote.{remote}.push doesn't include {branch}, so a plain push doesn't send it. Use Push to instead.
branch_push.plain.not_on_remote: push.default is matching, and {remote} has no {branch} as last fetched, so a plain push doesn't send it. Use Push to instead.
branch_push.plain.not_upstream_remote: push.default is upstream, and {key} sends {branch} to {remote} rather than {upstream_remote}, where its upstream {upstream} is. Git refuses that push. Use Push to, or set push.default to simple or current.
branch_push.plain.nothing: push.default is "nothing", so a plain git push pushes only what it is told to and {branch} isn't sent. Use Push to, or set push.default to simple.
